identity.title: Equilibrium Pricing in Oligopolistic Data Markets

problem.claim: The paper studies equilibrium pricing when strategic data sellers compete for budget-constrained buyers in oligopolistic data markets.

gap.claim: Unlike rivalrous goods, data’s non-rivalry can prevent exact Nash equilibrium and even a 1.364-approximate equilibrium under uniform pricing.

contributions.claim: Shows that uniform pricing may lack exact and 1.364-approximate Nash equilibria in non-rivalrous data markets.
Introduces piecewise-linear convex pricing and reports existence of a pricing profile in which no seller can improve revenue by a factor of two by deviating to any uniform price.
Reports simulations with fast convergence and empirical approximation guarantees better than the worst-case factor of 2.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish equilibrium pricing for non-rivalrous data from competitive-equilibrium intuition for rivalrous goods and propose beyond-uniform pricing to recover approximate stability.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that no 1.364-approximate equilibrium exists under uniform pricing.
The authors report existence of a pricing profile where no seller can improve revenue by a factor of two by deviating to any uniform price.
The authors report fast simulation convergence and empirical guarantees outperforming the factor-2 worst-case bound.

narrative_sequence.summary: Defines oligopolistic data-market pricing with budget-constrained buyers and strategic sellers.
Argues that data’s non-rivalry fundamentally changes equilibrium existence: uniform pricing may have neither exact nor 1.364-approximate equilibrium.
Investigates relaxed equilibrium notions and beyond-uniform piecewise-linear convex pricing.
Simulations reportedly converge quickly and achieve empirical approximation guarantees better than the worst-case factor of 2.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns a negative result for a restricted pricing class with a constructive guarantee after expanding the allowed pricing form.

lessons.interpretation: This pairing makes the motivation for the proposed relaxation directly traceable to the identified obstruction.
lessons.application: When presenting a new mechanism, first state the failure boundary of the baseline and then specify which added flexibility enables the claimed guarantee.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the baseline does not have a clearly stated failure mode or the proposed flexibility is not tied to a formal guarantee.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the market model, buyer budget assumptions, or conditions underlying the 1.364 impossibility result.
Details of the existence argument, simulations, convergence metric, and empirical approximation procedure are not provided.
